2230.heavy: Source calls Galo 'a weight/quantity-sensitive language (i.e., it treats “heavy” and “light” syllables differently)', but weight governs only how the unstressed final syllable reduces (CVV length neutralised phrase-finally; short final vowels and CVC nuclei reduced phrase-medially). 'Light' = 'CV- or V-' (sec. 6.2.1.1); heavy implicitly CVV/CVC (bimoraic phonological word, sec. 6.2.1.2). Accent placement is stated to be quantity-insensitive.
2230.prule: Stress accent on the initial syllable of the phonological word (prototypically disyllabic, bimoraic minimum): a trochaic strong-weak meter 'at the level of the phonological word'. Placement is explicitly quantity-insensitive ('whether heavy or light'); only the weak final syllable undergoes syncope/apocope and vowel reduction, and how it reduces depends on its weight and on phrase position.
2230.srule: Not mentioned in Post 2011 (secs. 6-6.3, pp. 210-215). Post 2007 (the reference grammar Post 2011 summarises): the phonological word is a single left-headed disyllabic foot, so there is no word-internal secondary stress; strings longer than two syllables are generally phonological phrases in which trochaic feet are built again ('foot-formation seems to apply a second time at the level of a phonological phrase'), lexeme-initial syllables being more prominent than stressed non-initial syllables and functors; 'primary' and 'secondary' stresses are not marked in the description.

2230.exq_: Importantly, however, only the final syllables of a disyllabic phonological word are affected; initial syllables of disyllabic phonological words, whether heavy or light, receive a stress accent and do not undergo any restructuring processes.
2230.tone: Same article, sec. 6.1 p.210: modern Tani languages are 'tonal at the level of the phonological word (Galo lagdú ‘forearm’, dunàm ‘to dig with a tool’…)'. Post 2015 (Tones in Northeast Indian languages) and the 2009 Galo-English Dictionary front matter describe two lexical word tones (H/L, 'Plain' vs 'Tense') spreading over the whole phonological word; Hyman 2007 cites Galo after Post 2007 as an /L, 0/ system. A two-tone word-tone system and the trochaic initial stress accent thus coexist on the same domain (the phonological word); none of these works states a rule relating tone to stress. Coded fixed and quantity-insensitive rather than tonal because the source states a stress-placement rule.

Hayward 1994 / Hayward & Chabo 2014 (tonal-accent analysis, quoted verbatim in Thomassen sec. 6.2): exactly one H per tone phrase, on the first word; H docks on the first lexically accented mora, otherwise by default on the ultima stem syllable of nouns/adjectives (Hayward 1994: the terminal vowel) or the first post-thematic syllable of verbs; a word in isolation is its own phrase, so every citation form carries one H; H spreads 1-2 morae rightward within the phrasal word. 2231.tone: Hayward 1994 and Hayward & Chabo 2014 call Gamo a 'tonal-accent language' (Hayward 1990 n.17 prefers 'tonal accent' to 'pitch accent'): one culminative, obligatory H per tone phrase, position lexical (accented root mora) or default (ultima stem syllable / terminal vowel of nominals; first post-thematic syllable of verbs). 2232.tone: Gǁana (Gyom dialect, New Xade) has four lexical tones H/M/L/falling marked on each vowel or syllabic nasal in fully tone-marked sentence data (Sekere et al. 2023, appendix p. 9). The companion paper Sekere, Kato, Ono & Nakagawa 2025 [2026], Gǁana data: voice, JILR 30(48), p. 3 (Japanese) states that some transitive/intransitive pairs are distinguished by lexically determined tonal alternation, khóán 'break (tr.)' vs khôān 'break (intr.)'. No opened Gǁana source mentions stress, accent or prominence (a full-text search of all saved text files: zero hits for 'stress'; 'accent' only as the grave accent in Nakagawa 1996 on Gǀui). The closest first-hand prominence statement is for the mutually intelligible sister language Gǀui (gwii1239), Nakagawa 2006 PhD, Ch. 2 §2.2.2.3 p. 42: 'Another prosodic property is what I call here "prominence", which is involved in DOM1. Roots are always pronounced with certain auditory "prominence", which non-roots lack. This prominence involves a relatively wide pitch range, as well as loudness and length.' Table 2.3: DOM1 = lexical root, always bimoraic, three tones, prominence +; DOM2 = grammatical non-root, typically monomoraic, two tones, prominence -. Ch. 2 later: 'In my auditory impression, prominence attenuates in running speech.' This is a root-domain (morphological/tonal-domain) prominence inside a three-tone system, not a positional word-stress rule, and it is not a statement about Gǁana proper.

2233.prule: Nanchang Gan is a five-tone language (42, 24, 45, 213, 21). Word-level 'lexical stress' is a full-syllable vs light-syllable (qingsheng) contrast: a lexically stressless light syllable can only be the second syllable of a disyllabic word (strong-weak), and which words have a full-light shape is not predictable by any rule but lexically specified (minimal pair toŋ42 ɕi42 'east west' vs toŋ42 ɕi 'thing'); in full-full words native speakers cannot tell which syllable is more stressed. vlen.q: There are three types of syllables in Nanchang: CV (C = Consonant; V = Vowel); CVR (R = Sonorant consonant); and CVO (O = Obstruent). There is no vowel length contrast in Nanchang.

tn.quote: There are five lexical tones in Nanchang. It consists of two types of stress and three syllable types. ... There are five lexical tones in Nanchang, traditionally transcribed as 42 (yinping), 24 (yangping), 45 (yinqu), 213 (shang), and 21 (yangqu). All five tones can be realized on CV and CVR syllables. On CVO syllables, the tonal inventory is reduced to 5 (yin ru) and 2 (yang ru) (Li 1995). Therefore, in Nanchang, syllable types restrict tonal contrasts. ... we argue that the sonorous rhyme in a syllable is the tone bearing unit.

2234.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word by default; a non-initial syllable containing a long vowel receives primary stress instead (weight = phonemic vowel length; any non-initial position, since long vowels are never final and never in affixes). Secondary stress on the penultimate syllable. Compound stems: primary on the first syllable, secondary on the first syllable of each subsequent morpheme; a reduplicated morpheme also receives primary stress.
2234.srule: Secondary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (a single secondary stress; Keen gives no examples and does not discuss short words where the penult is the initial syllable or adjacent to the primary). In compound stems, secondary stress on the first syllable of each non-initial morpheme (a reduplicated morpheme takes primary stress instead).
2234.quote: 2.3 STRESS. Stress can be predicted according to the following rules. Primary stress falls on the first syllable and secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word except for the following modifications: (i) a non-initial syllable containing a long vowel receives primary stress. (ii) Words with compound stems have primary stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on the first syllable of each subsequent morpheme unless it is a reduplicated morpheme in which case it also receives primary stress.

2235.tone: Kerbs 2019 ch. 4: three underlying tones (11 L, 35 R, 55 H); two surface tones on isolation monosyllables, three on first syllables of disyllables; word-final syllables largely neutralized by dissimilation -- after a L first syllable the final is H (55) or R (35) ('syllables belonging to the tone categories A, B, and D can surface as either /55/ or /35/ following a L tone syllable, while C syllables are always /55/ in this position', p. 64), after a H (C) first syllable the final is L (11): 'If the first syllable is C, the expected tone sequence is H-L (55-11)' (p. 64); dissimilation 'sometimes fails to apply for reasons that are not known at present, especially in reading pronunciations' (p. 64). Reduced (destressed, monomoraic) syllables are more frequent than the Standard Mandarin neutral tone and not confined to word-final position (sec. 4.1). Kerbs 2021: 24 suggests the tonal domain may be larger than the syllable with the first syllable tone-bearing (toneless perfect particle -lio takes its pitch from the preceding syllable; compared to Shanghai). Stress is mentioned only as an uninvestigated factor ('may play an important role', p. 67; 'stress or tone deletion', p. 64); the word 'stress' does not occur in Kerbs 2021. Janhunen 2007: 97 ('tones... seem to have been lost in both Wutun and Gangou') is second-hand and hedged, superseded by Kerbs's first-hand data.

2237.dloc: Haurholm-Larsen 2016, Sec. 2.3 'Stress', pp. 22-23; Sec. 2.1.1 p. 16 on accent marking; Sec. 2.4 p. 23 on light/heavy syllables; Sec. 7.6 intro on clitics and secondary stress. JIPA 2023 'Prosodic features' p. 394.
2237.heavy: Sec. 2.4 defines a V/CV syllable (short or long, oral or nasal vowel) as 'a light syllable' and C1VC2 with C2 = /y/ or /w/ as 'a heavy syllable', but no stress rule refers to syllable weight.
2237.prule: Primary stress is lexically determined and contrastive (ábürüha 'fall' vs abûrüha 'write'), restricted to a two-syllable window at the left edge of the phonological word (initial or second syllable). Verb stems keep their lexical stress under affixation; affixes and clitics never bear primary stress.
2237.srule: Secondary stress exists (grave accent in the grammar's orthography) and is not distinctive, but its placement is not given: 'much less predictable and I have yet to figure out which generalizations can be made regarding its distribution' (Sec. 2.3); elsewhere 'assigned according to regular metric rules (Taylor, 1955; Cayetano, 1992)' (Sec. 7.6), rules not restated. Affixes and clitics may carry secondary (never primary) stress; passives take secondary stress on the stem-final syllable before -wa (Sec. 6.1.2.1).

2240.prule: Word stress is on the final syllable by default (nominals, plural -ā́, infinitive -mún, past participle -é), but a listed set of verbal affixes takes the stress off the final syllable: the Set1 person endings of the present (stress on the ending, before the unstressed durative -e: xunā́ne, xunéme), the participial element -é- of the imperfect (xunté-m-e), the prefix bé- or a preverb in the subjunctive (and, per the Tense Markers section, imperative/preterit/perfect), and the negative ná-; preverbs attract stress (mālúe 'he rubs' vs. vár-mālue 'he flees'). Stress placement is therefore set by morpheme class (Persian/Central-Dialect type), not by syllable count or weight.

tn.quote: Like most Nigerian languages, Gbari is a tone language and every vowel can have one of five possible tones. There are three level tones and two glides, rising and falling. The glide tones are rare and they could be analysed as combinations of level tones. However, they seem to occur in isolation on some words which indicates that they must be treated as separate tonemes. The tones are shown as follows; High @ Mid Unmarked Low $ Rising ^ Falling & When words are different only in tone, they are listed in the order low, middle, high.

tn.note: Five tonemes on every vowel: three level (high, mid, low) plus rare rising and falling glides, kept as separate tonemes though possibly level sequences; syllabic nasals bear tone. Nothing on stress.

2245.dq: Word stress is relatively light, falling regularly on the ultima, with secondary stress in longer words.
2245.dloc: p. 856, sect. 7.4.5.4.2.2 'Phonology'; page rendered and read as image.
2245.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable (ultima) of the word, quantity-insensitive; the stressable word = root plus any personal possessive suffix (nouns) or personal object suffix (verbs), stress falling on the final syllable of those suffixes when present. A listed set of outer suffixes -- clause markers (the 'time-mood-aspect' suffixes) on verbs, locative and instrumental suffixes on nouns -- is never stressed, so a word ending in one of them keeps stress on the last syllable before it. Stress is phonetically 'relatively light'.
2245.srule: Exists, placement not given: 'with secondary stress in longer words' (Freyberg 1977: 856); the source does not say where the secondary stress falls.
2245.quote: Word stress is relatively light, falling regularly on the ultima, with secondary stress in longer words. The ultimate stress is not restricted to the root, but on nouns it falls on the final syllable of personal possessive suffixes, and on verbs it shifts to the final syllable of personal object suffixes. Other suffixes, such as clause markers on verbs and locative and instrumental suffixes on nouns, are never stressed.

2246.prule: Tone language: lexically distinctive pitch on every syllable (Bolé-Richard 1983: two tonemes HAUT/BAS, the only 'necessary' prosodic feature being 'ton'; Lotven 2020: tonemes L, H, marginal HL; Henrici 1891: three 'Tonstufen' Hochton/Tiefton/Tonlosigkeit; Seidel 1904 sec. 10: rising vs falling 'Intonation' distinguishing homophones). No modern description states or denies word stress. In addition, the pre-tonological descriptions state that word accent ('Wortton', 'accento') falls on the final syllable of polysyllabic words in citation form, hedged ('in der Regel' Henrici; 'meist' Seidel) and, per de Gregorio, levelled in connected speech; de Gregorio files this under 'Tonalità' and uses it to justify omitting tone marks. Only two of these are first-hand: Henrici 1891 (Gbe-wide: Anlo, Anecho, Dahome) and de Gregorio 1901 (Anecho informant). Seidel 1904 Part II is compiled from written sources (p. 39 fn. 1 'Gebrauchte Quellen' lists Henrici 1891 first), so 'Der Wortton liegt meist auf der Endsilbe' is a Gen-specific restatement of Henrici, not an independent observation.

2246.tone: All sources treat Gen as a tone language. Bolé-Richard 1983: 118 (excerpt) 'Le Gen a deux tonèmes HAUT et BAS qui sont des traits syllabiques oppositionnels'; p. 105 (excerpt) lists the necessary prosodic features as 'ton' and 'syllabicité' only; a search for 'accent tonique' in the book returns 0 hits. Lotven 2020 sec. 6: L, H and marginal HL tonemes, HL in ideophones/interjections/loans, French loans with final stress borrowed with final HL (p. 20); no mention of stress otherwise. Henrici 1891: 18 names three musical 'Tonstufen' (Hochton, Tiefton, Tonlosigkeit) that decide word meaning; Seidel 1904: 40 sec. 10 says homophones are sometimes distinguished by 'Intonation', rising vs falling tone of a vowel; de Gregorio 1901: 145 files his final-accent remark under 'Tonalità'. On stress: the two first-hand historical observers (Henrici, de Gregorio) plus Seidel's compilation state final-syllable word accent in citation forms (hedged); the historical 'Ton'/'Wortton' is not separated from pitch (Henrici's demonstratives ehe, esi, eke have 'Ton' on the first syllable, i.e. the prefix vowel, which reads as a tonal, not a stress, observation). Modern descriptions are does not discuss stress (no positive or negative statement in Lotven 2020, Lotven & Berkson 2019, or the Bolé-Richard/Gblem-Poidi/Kangni/Capo excerpt).

2249.prule: quantity-insensitive, quantity-insensitive: disyllabic left-headed (trochaic) feet are parsed from the left edge of the word, a leftover word-final syllable is extrametrical, and primary stress falls on the head of the rightmost foot. Result: initial stress in 2- and 3-syllable words, penultimate stress in even-syllable words of 4+, antepenultimate stress in odd-syllable words of 5+ (e.g. /ˌkadiˈkita/, /ˌataˈkamana/). Non-final foot heads carry secondary stress. Equivalent to 'penult in even-count words, antepenult in odd-count words'.
2249.srule: In words of four or more syllables, secondary stress falls on the first syllable and on every alternate syllable to the right (heads of the non-final disyllabic feet parsed from the left edge), primary stress on the rightmost foot: /,kadi'kita/ 'mortar', /,ata'kamana/ 'door' (p. 53). In prefixed/encliticised words: the disyllabic reciprocal prefix /βari-/ is its own foot with secondary stress on its first syllable (p. 54); when a polysyllabic enclitic takes primary stress on a root of more than two syllables, the secondary foot is aligned to the left edge of the root and unfooted syllables in between are extrametrical, e.g. /,dogoro='ria/ 'look=3PL.OBJ' (p. 55).
2249.quote: The phonological foot in Kubokota consists of two syllables. Words are parsed from left to right; any syllables at the right edge of the word that cannot be assigned to feet are extrametrical. Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot. 2250.heavy: A long vowel produced by contraction of two like vowels (after a suffix is added or an intervocalic consonant drops); in a final syllable or a monosyllable it carries the accent ('accent circonflexe': donâ < donáa, kisâ < kisáa, kô < kóo).
2250.prule: Primary ('acute') accent on the penultimate syllable of every word, computed from syllable count with no reference to syllable weight; monosyllables carry it; short grammatical particles (articles, prepositions, conjunctions: a, ko, na, i, ta, ma) are unaccented. The accent is dynamically weak with a slight pitch rise on the strong syllable. Suffixation keeps the accent penultimate (lábu 'strike' > labúa 'strike him'; tóbo 'float' > tóbolaginía 'make it float').
2250.srule: Hedged by the author ('il semble'): in words with several stacked monosyllabic suffixes or a polysyllabic suffix, where the main accent moves to the penult of the whole form, a secondary accent remains on the syllable that is accented in the bare base (tóbo > tóbolaginía 'make it float'; lábu > weilabúgi 'they fight'). No secondary or rhythmic accent is described for unsuffixed words.

2251.dq: Der Akzent ist unbeweglich; er ruht immer auf derselben Silbe in allen Formen und zum Teil auch Ableitungen eines Wortes (p. 47); contrasted with sentence accent on p. 48: 'Vereinzelte Fälle ... erklären sich aus dem Satzakzent, durch Analogiewirkung u. a.'; Lowman 1932: 272: 'Not every syllable stressed in isolation need bear the sentence stress.'

2251.prule: One accent per word, fixed on the stem and immobile under inflection and in part ('zum Teil') also under derivation: mál 'mountain', def. máli, gen.-dat. pl. máleve. Within base words (Grundwoerter) the accent is on the final syllable; penultimate accent only in defined classes: feminines in -ë, -e, -o (púnë, núse, víto), adjectives and other words in -ë (i bárdhë, pírë), and the unstressed suffixes -ës, -ën, -zë, -ur, -un, -të, -tas, -a, -ëń. All other base words and suffixes are oxytone (kunát, çobán, besník, Shqipëtár, punëtúar; verbs kërkój, gënéj, godís, bërtás); so masculines and verbs are oxytone, feminines paroxytone. Because inflection usually adds one syllable and feminines are numerous, the majority of surface word forms are paroxytone (hence the Albanologists' convention of leaving penult stress unmarked). Gheg and Tosk accent the same syllable. Gheg-internal confirmations: Lowman 1932: 272 (Shkoder) 'It may be given to any syllable of a word, but usually falls on the penult... In a particular word the stress does not vary with the different inflectional forms but remains fixed on the same syllable'; Pisko 1896: 2 (Shkoder) 'Der Ton der meisten albanesischen Worte liegt auf der vorletzten Silbe'; Weigand 1913: 6 (South Gheg) accent written only when not on the penult, long/nasal vowels always carry it.
2251.srule: Only in compounds and at sentence level. Lowman 1932 (Shkodër Gheg): three degrees of stress, but 'The secondary stress-accent occurs in some words, chiefly compounds, when they are pronounced in isolation' (kundërshtim [ˌkunr̥ˈʃtim], secondary on the first member); otherwise 'secondary' is a sentence-rhythm grade. No rhythmic secondary stress in simplex words: Pekmezi 1908 sec. 24 posits no secondary accent and only grades the unstressed syllables (the syllable next to the tonic is the weakest; trisyllabic oxytone 1½: 1: 3).

2251.tone: Pekmezi p. 47, opening of sec. 22: the Albanian accent is in general expiratory, but in Gheg the musical element comes out strongly ('tritt im Gegischen das musikalische Element stark hervor'); the pitch movement in long syllables is falling, notably in Gheg monophthongs derived from diphthongs. Adeniyi 2012: L and M are downstepped; speakers can suppress downstep by discourse factors. 2253.tone: §120 p. 76: 'hat auch das Nuba... den musikalischen Silbenton'; tones are bound to the word form, contrasted with expressive 'Ausdruckstöne', and change meaning. §123 p. 78: only two pitch levels a fourth apart (Hochton c, Tiefton g in the consultant's voice) plus two glides, Hochtiefton and Tiefhochton. tn.quote: Previously word stress in Gilaki was described as purely dynamic (Rastorgueva et al. 2012: 19, 1971: 27, Rastorgueva 1999b: 115). In 2015 a further study was conducted on the Gilaki language. The speech of three men and one woman was recorded; 41 two-syllable words (82 syllables) with initial and final stress were analyzed. The experiment showed that word stress in Gilaki is two- componential – tonal-dynamic12. Pitch is a more reliable indicator in this process: on average it is 9.4% higher in the stressed syllable (Sig<0.001), while intensity rises only by 2.3% (Sig=0.006).

The source describes Ginyanga as a two-tone language (high vs. low; tone-bearing unit = one vowel; syllabic /n/ bears tone) with lexical tone contrasts (wù 'see!' vs wú 'die!'; nàrɩ̀ 'spider' vs nárɩ́ 'ox') and grammatical tone (IPFV prefix H; PFV prefix L+H). Word stress, accent or rhythmic prominence is not mentioned anywhere in the 41-page sketch.
2256.quote: 2.2. Tones Ginyanga has two phonological tones: high and low. A tone-bearing unit contains only one vowel. Consider examples (15)-(16) where segmentally identical words with different tones have different lexical meanings. (15) wù ‘see!’ (imperative) – wú ‘die!’ (imperative) (16) nàrɩ̀ ‘spider’ – nárɩ́ ‘ox’ A nasal /n/ can bear tones. See, for instance, that ń- is a high-toned 1sg Imperfective prefix (17) (§3.3.2) in opposition to ǹ-, a low-toned cl6 prefix (18) (§3.1), while [ŋ̀], a variant of /n/ that might be the result of a contraction, is a high-toned 1sg Future prefix (19) (§3.3.3). ...…

2256.idn: Ginyanga (self-designation of speakers: anyanga), North Guang, Kwa; glottocode giny1241, ISO ayg; data: Agbandi (largest Anyanga village), Prefecture of Blitta, Central Togo; consultants from Agbandi and Diguina; four field trips 2019-2024 (five months total); corpus collected 2019-2024
2256.tone: Two level tones H and L; TBU = a single vowel (vowel sequences are biphonemic, each vowel its own TBU, cf. PFV prefix ɔ̀ɔ́-); syllabic nasal /n/ bears tone (ń- 1sg.IPFV H vs ǹ- cl6 L). Tone is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs 15-16) and grammatically contrastive (IPFV H prefix vs PFV L-H prefix). The sketch says nothing about stress, accent, prominence or rhythm; 'prominence' occurs only for discourse prominence (focus markers, sec. 3.8). Sister sources say the same or less: Aplonova 2025 PhD sec. 2.1.2 p. 31 ('Ginyanga has two phonological tones: high and low... A tone bearing unit contains only one vowel... The nasal /n/ bears tones when it is followed by a consonant'), prosody of complex predicates explicitly 'non analysee'; Pozdniakova & Aplonova 2024 ('Ginyanga is a tonal language, with two structural tones'); Pozdniakova & Aplonova 2022 p. 244 ('Ginyanga is a tonal language that has presumably high and low phonemic level tones'); Pozdniakova 2021 fn. 1 (tonal language like other Kwa languages, tone system understudied, examples untonemarked). No source denies word stress, so this is 'tone system, no stress rule', not no word stress.

tn.quote: Ginyanga has two phonological tones: high and low. A tone-bearing unit contains only one vowel. Consider examples (15)-(16) where segmentally identical words with different tones have different lexical meanings. (15) wù ‘see!’ (imperative) – wú ‘die!’ (imperative) (16) nàrɩ̀ ‘spider’ – nárɩ́ ‘ox’ A nasal /n/ can bear tones. ... Tones are also used to distinguish between the basic aspectual opposition of Imperfective vs. Perfective. The Imperfective prefix has a high tone (20), while the first vowel of the Perfective has a low tone and the second one has a high tone (21).
